passage: Four software teams each found their own way with AI tools. Bhavna, a team lead, wrote a short list. Writing first versions of tests and condensing published documents were fine, while pasting customer data or company secrets into open tools was not. Sachin's team tried the tools for a month, but only on documentation and drafts of unit tests. They measured how much time was saved and how many errors crept in, and only afterwards thought about using them on important code. A junior developer on another team merged code written by AI without reading it. It held an insecure query that passed the basic tests and reached the live system before a reviewer spotted it. Sangeeta's team once found a wrong figure in an AI-written report. They traced how it slipped past review, added a check step, changed their rules, and began regarding the tool as a coworker who can be mistaken.

qa.q: What did Sachin's team measure during their month of trying the tools?
qa.a: They measured how much time was saved and how many errors crept in.

qa.q: How does the junior developer's handling of AI code differ from Sangeeta's team's handling of the wrong figure, and what changed?
qa.a: The junior merged code unread, so an insecure query reached the live system. Sangeeta's team traced how the error passed review and added a check step, so the process improved.

qa.q: What might the junior developer be feeling after the reviewer finds the insecure query?
qa.a: They are probably embarrassed and worried, having trusted the tool without checking.

qa.q: What could the junior developer do from now on?
qa.a: They could read and test every piece of AI-written code, and ask a reviewer to look at anything unfamiliar before it merges. 🙂

grounding: Four teams work with AI tools by setting limits, piloting on low-risk tasks, trusting output without review, and reviewing an incident.
